Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits
Against Reward Hacking in GRPO

Shurun Li Affiliation: REASONS Lab, Institute for Network Sciences and Cyberspace, Tsinghua University    Michael Hua Wang Affiliation: REASONS Lab, Institute for Network Sciences and Cyberspace, Tsinghua University    Haibo Zeng Affiliation: Virginia Tech{lisr22, wanghua24}@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn, hbzeng@vt.edu, longwang@tsinghua.edu.cn    Long Wang Affiliation: REASONS Lab, Institute for Network Sciences and Cyberspace, Tsinghua University
Preprint, October 2026
Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains on cheap checks, such as unit tests, that a policy can learn to game, while a stronger check is too expensive to run on every rollout. We study how to spend a limited strong-verifier budget in GRPO, separating which weakly passing rollouts to audit from what reward a caught hack receives. At a fixed policy state with centered advantages, the expected update depends on a design only through each rollout’s marginal audit probability and correction; reflecting a caught hack’s reward about the failure reward negates the advantages of an all-hack group; and auditing whole groups with the fewest weak passes first (low-pass budgeted audits, LB) minimizes the advantage mass left on hacks among pass-count designs with a fixed correction when a label’s value falls with the pass count. We tested this analysis in actual LLM training: from each run’s starting state, the sign of this mass on a frozen panel predicted whether hacking would be suppressed in 33 of 39 runs, including 13 of 16 preregistered ones. In LeetCode (Wong et al., 2026) and Countdown-Code (Khalifa et al., 2026), LB drives hacking to near zero, while random audits with the same penalty and budget do not and use more labels. We also find that the randomness of the update affects training: in Countdown-Code, two unbiased corrections, per-item reward-level IPW and a group-level advantage correction, bring hacking down too but end 6.1–11.8 and 8.0–11.5 points lower in held-out accuracy than LB at the same budget. A full audit, which the group-level correction reproduces in expectation, stays within about two points of LB in three seeds, while LB uses 28% of its labels, and allocating the same correction by pass count recovers most of the loss (one seed). Training outcomes thus depend not only on the expected update but also on the randomness of its estimate.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models on automatic checks such as unit tests, and a policy can learn to pass a weak check without solving the task. In Countdown-Code it rewrites the target value in its own solution file so that the provided test passes (Khalifa et al., 2026); in the LeetCode environment of Wong et al. (2026) it defines its own run_tests function, which the grader then executes. A stronger check, such as the full test suite or a semantic check of the answer, is usually available, but it costs too much to run on every rollout (Wang et al., 2025; Sakib et al., 2026).

This paper asks how to spend a fixed strong-verifier budget during group-relative policy optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024). An audit design makes two choices: which weakly passing rollouts to send to the strong verifier (selection) and what reward a caught hack receives (correction). Two defaults are natural: random audits with an inverse-propensity correction, which reproduce the full-audit reward in expectation (Horvitz and Thompson, 1952; Moya et al., 2026; Sakib et al., 2026), and giving a caught hack the reward its strong verdict implies. Neither accounts for how GRPO turns rewards into updates. A rollout’s advantage depends on its siblings, so the same caught hack can push the policy strongly, weakly, or not at all.

We make three observations. First, without group standard-deviation normalization, the expected raw policy gradient depends on an audit design only through each rollout’s marginal audit probability and correction value (Lemma 1): coupling audits within groups changes the noise of an update, while selection and correction change its direction. Second, giving a caught hack the reward 2​b−a2b-a, the pass reward aa reflected about the failure reward bb, exactly negates the advantages of a group whose weak passes are all hacks, whereas the strong-verdict reward bb only zeroes them (Proposition 1, Figure 2b). Third, an uncaught hack’s advantage is largest when few siblings pass, so a label spent on a low-pass group buys the most correction (Figure 2a). Low-pass budgeted audits (LB) therefore audit whole groups in increasing order of weak passes until a fixed fraction pp of the batch’s weak passes has been checked in expectation (Figure 1a). Among whole-group designs that select by pass count and give caught hacks a fixed correction, LB minimizes a frozen-state objective, the advantage mass left on hacks, whenever the value of a label does not increase with the pass count (Theorem 1).

We test these designs in two reward-hacking environments from prior work, LeetCode (Wong et al., 2026) with LoRA training of Qwen3-4B and Countdown-Code (Khalifa et al., 2026) with full fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-3B, starting from checkpoints where about a quarter of the training rollouts are hacks. Every comparison was preregistered. Our contributions follow three steps:

  • •

    When the push on hacks is optimal (Section 3). The three observations above characterize how an audit design changes the expected update at a frozen policy state, and LB minimizes the advantage mass left on hacks among whole-group pass-count designs with a fixed correction whenever a label’s value does not increase with the pass count (Theorem 1).

  • •

    Predicting training from the frozen push (Section 5). With the same penalty and budget rule, LB drives LeetCode hacking to near zero within about ten steps in all three seeds, while auditing groups in random order leaves late hacking at 36.33–51.68% and auditing single weak passes at random at 45.62–55.78%, with LB using about half their labels; random group order also fails in Countdown-Code (one seed; Section 5.1). The correction value matters as much: the strong-verdict reward c=bc=b only removes the push on a caught all-hack group, and with it auditing the lowest-pass groups is no better than auditing random groups, whereas with 2​b−a2b-a the same groups remove hacking with half the labels (Section 5.2). From each run’s starting state, the sign of the frozen hack mass JJ predicted whether hacking would be suppressed in 33 of 39 runs, including 13 of 16 preregistered ones. The push stops predicting in two places: an online rule that improved JJ on frozen panels trained worse than LB, so the magnitude of JJ does not rank designs, and with c=bc=b hacking spread beyond the low-pass groups (Section 5.4).

  • •

    Beyond the expected update, randomness affects training (Section 6). In Countdown-Code, per-item reward-level inverse-propensity weighting (IPW) and a group-level advantage correction (Sakib et al., 2026) also suppress hacking, but in all three seeds end lower than LB in training correctness (by 4.53–11.13 and 3.48–9.92 pp) and in held-out accuracy (by 6.1–11.8 and 8.0–11.5 pp); in LeetCode the group-level correction was close to LB. A full audit, which every unbiased group-level design matches in expectation on a frozen batch, stayed within about two points of LB on held-out problems in all three seeds while LB used 28% of its labels, and allocating the group-level correction by pass count closed most of the gap (one seed). Its loss therefore comes from the randomness of the estimate and the allocation of audits, not from the full-audit update it targets.

Relation to budgeted audit estimation.

Sakib et al. (2026) study unbiased estimation of full-suite training signals on fixed software-engineering trajectories, including a direct correction of normalized group advantages, and target groups with more passes to reduce estimator variance. We study how selection and correction affect on-policy learning, and target groups with fewer passes first, where an uncaught hack is reinforced the most. Our comparisons cover two unbiased corrections at matched budgets: per-item reward-level IPW and the group-level advantage correction.

2 Setup

Weak and strong verifiers.

For each prompt GRPO samples a group of KK responses. The weak verifier gives reward aa to a response it accepts (a weak pass), bb to a well-formed response it rejects, and 00 to a malformed one, with 0≤b<a0\leq b<a. A strong verifier, run only on weak passes, decides whether a weak pass is genuine. Every strong pass is a weak pass, so responses fall into three classes: correct (C: weak and strong pass), hack (H: weak pass, strong fail), and failure (F: weak fail). In Countdown-Code (a,b)=(1.2,0.2)(a,b)=(1.2,0.2); in LeetCode (a,b)=(3.5,0.5)(a,b)=(3.5,0.5), which is 3.0 for passing the tests plus 0.5 for compiling. We assume the strong verifier is reliable and its errors are independent of the policy; Section 8 discusses this assumption.

Group-relative advantages.

With rewards r1,…,rKr_{1},\dots,r_{K}, GRPO uses Ai=(ri−r¯)/(σ+ϵ)A_{i}=(r_{i}-\bar{r})/(\sigma+\epsilon), where r¯\bar{r} and σ\sigma are the group mean and unbiased standard deviation (“group std”) and Ai=0A_{i}=0 when σ=ϵ=0\sigma=\epsilon=0, or the centered Ai=ri−r¯A_{i}=r_{i}-\bar{r} (“no std”; Liu et al., 2025). In both of our environments, training uses a clipped surrogate (Schulman et al., 2017) with token-mean aggregation (Yu et al., 2025). To first order at the sampling policy, a batch moves the parameters along g=∑iAi​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣xi)g=\sum_{i}A_{i}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x_{i}), up to positive per-response weights that depend only on the batch.

Audit designs.

An audit design selects a set MM of weak passes for the strong verifier and replaces the reward of each caught hack i∈M∩Hi\in M\cap H by a correction value. The budget is a fraction pp of the batch’s WW weak passes in expectation, 𝔼​|M|=p​W\mathbb{E}|M|=pW. With a fixed pp the spend follows WW, the number of correct responses plus hacks, so it falls only when weak passes fall. We compare the following selection rules.

  • •

    LB (low-pass budgeted): groups with at least one weak pass are sorted by their number of weak passes kk, with ties broken at random. Whole groups are audited in this order while they fit in the remaining budget; the first group that does not fit is audited with probability equal to the remaining budget divided by its kk. The expected cost is exactly p​WpW.

  • •

    RB (random budgeted): the same rule with the groups in random order.

  • •

    Random items: each weak pass is audited independently with probability pp, and a caught hack receives the correction cc itself; the expected cost matches RB’s, but audits within a group are not coupled.

  • •

    IPW (per item): each weak pass is audited independently with probability pp, and a caught hack receives a+(c−a)/pa+(c-a)/p, so its expected reward is cc: the design is unbiased for a full audit with correction cc at the reward level, and with centered advantages also for the raw gradient (Lemma 1) (Horvitz and Thompson, 1952).

  • •

    Full audits every weak pass; None audits nothing. Two fixed-count variants used in LeetCode audit the 8 groups with the fewest weak passes (Low) or 8 random groups with at least one weak pass (Pos) at each step.

The correction value is either the strong-verdict reward c=bc=b, which treats a caught hack like any well-formed failure, or the reflected penalty c=2​b−ac=2b-a: −0.8-0.8 in Countdown-Code and −2.5-2.5 in LeetCode. For IPW, the reflected target gives a caught hack 1.2+(−0.8−1.2)/0.28=−5.941.2+(-0.8-1.2)/0.28=-5.94 in Countdown-Code.

Metrics.

For measurement only, the strong verifier labels every training rollout. The hack rate hth_{t} is the fraction of rollouts at step tt in class H, and correctness CtC_{t} the fraction in class C. We report AUC⁡(h)\mathrm{AUC}(h), the mean of hth_{t} over the 40 training steps; the hack rate, correctness and pass@KK over the late window of steps 31–40; the number of strong labels used for training (audited weak passes, summed over training); and the number of generated tokens. Trained checkpoints from the main comparisons and key ablations are also evaluated on held-out test problems. Unless stated otherwise, differences are in percentage points (pp), first arm minus second.

3 How audit designs change the update

We analyze a single training step at the sampling policy: the batch, its weak rewards and its classes are fixed, and the audit design is the only source of randomness (Theorems 1 and 2 also average over group compositions given pass counts). Proofs and further results are in Appendices A and B.

3.1 Selection and correction change the direction; coupling changes the noise

Let mi∈{0,1}m_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicate that weak pass ii is audited, with marginal probability πi=Pr⁡(mi=1)\pi_{i}=\Pr(m_{i}=1) given the batch, and let cic_{i} be the reward a caught hack receives (ci=cc_{i}=c for a fixed penalty, ci=a+(c−a)/πic_{i}=a+(c-a)/\pi_{i} for IPW), fixed given the batch. The post-audit reward is ri=riw+mi 1[i∈H](ci−a)r_{i}=r^{w}_{i}+m_{i}\,\mathbf{1}[i\in H]\,(c_{i}-a).

Lemma 1 (Only marginals matter without std normalization).

With centered advantages Ai=ri−r¯A_{i}=r_{i}-\bar{r}, the expected raw policy gradient at a fixed state, 𝔼⁡[g]=∑i𝔼⁡[Ai]​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yi∣xi)\mathbb{E}[g]=\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}[A_{i}]\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x_{i}), depends on the design only through πi​(ci−a)\pi_{i}(c_{i}-a) for each hack ii. In particular, auditing whole groups and auditing items independently with the same marginals and the same correction give the same 𝔼⁡[g]\mathbb{E}[g], and IPW with target cc gives the same 𝔼⁡[g]\mathbb{E}[g] as auditing every weak pass with correction cc.

The lemma follows from linearity of the reward correction, the group mean and the sum over responses. With centered advantages, the unit of audit therefore affects only the noise of the raw gradient, which is what Sakib et al. (2026) measure, while its expectation changes only through which responses are likely to be audited and what a caught hack receives. Group std normalization breaks the lemma (Sections 3.4 and F); adaptive optimizers and gradient clipping break its corollary for parameter steps, which are nonlinear in gg.

3.2 The reflected penalty negates a two-valued group

Proposition 1 (Reflection).

Consider a group whose kk weak passes, 1≤k<K1\leq k<K, are all hacks and whose other responses all have reward bb, and suppose every weak pass is audited. If caught hacks receive c=2​b−ac=2b-a, the post-audit rewards are ri′=2​b−riwr^{\prime}_{i}=2b-r^{w}_{i}, so the advantages are exactly negated, Ai′=−AiwA^{\prime}_{i}=-A^{w}_{i}, with centered advantages and with std normalization for any ϵ\epsilon in the denominator. For a general c<bc<b, let λ=(b−c)/(a−b)\lambda=(b-c)/(a-b) and let σ\sigma be the group’s standard deviation before the audit; then Ai′=−λ​AiwA^{\prime}_{i}=-\lambda A^{w}_{i} with centered advantages and Ai′=−λ⁡(σ+ϵ)λ​σ+ϵ​AiwA^{\prime}_{i}=-\frac{\lambda(\sigma+\epsilon)}{\lambda\sigma+\epsilon}A^{w}_{i} with std normalization. If c=bc=b, all rewards in the group equal bb and every advantage is zero.

So the reflected penalty is the only fixed correction that turns the push toward the hacks in such a group into an equal and opposite push under both advantage forms; with std normalization and ϵ=0\epsilon=0, every c<bc<b does so. In LeetCode, which uses std normalization, LB with penalty −0.25-0.25 instead of −2.5-2.5 also suppressed hacking (one seed; Appendix I). The strong-verdict reward only removes the push, and a partially discounted reward b<c<ab<c<a, as in detector-based reward shaping, leaves the hacks with positive advantages (Anonymous, 2026). Whenever 2​b−a≤02b-a\leq 0, as in both of our environments, a caught hack has the lowest reward in any group and hence a non-positive advantage. In a mixed group, the group-adaptive correction 2​μN−a2\mu_{N}-a, with μN\mu_{N} the mean reward of the other responses, negates every hack’s advantage and keeps the other contrasts, but needs the strong labels of the whole group (Proposition 4).

3.3 The value of a label and low-pass budgeted audits

Consider whole-group designs at a frozen state. A design audits each group with kk weak passes with some probability, at an expected cost of kk labels per audited group. The objective is the expected advantage mass on hacks, 𝔼⁡[J]\mathbb{E}[J] with J=∑groups1K​∑i∈HAiJ=\sum_{\text{groups}}\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{i\in H}A_{i}, which an audit design should make as negative as possible. Write μk0\mu_{k}^{0} and μk1\mu_{k}^{1} for the expected value of 1K​∑i∈HAi\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i\in H}A_{i} in a kk-pass group when it is not audited and when it is fully audited, and define the value per label

dk=μk0−μk1k.d_{k}=\frac{\mu_{k}^{0}-\mu_{k}^{1}}{k}. (1)
Theorem 1 (Conditional optimality of LB).

Fix the pass counts of the groups in a batch, suppose each group’s composition is random with a distribution that depends only on its pass count and is independent of the design’s randomness, and let BB be the expected label budget (B=p​WB=pW). Consider whole-group designs that give every caught hack the same correction value, whose audit decisions depend only on the pass counts and on independent randomness, with expected cost at most BB. If dk≥0d_{k}\geq 0 for all kk and dkd_{k} is non-increasing in kk, then LB minimizes 𝔼⁡[J]\mathbb{E}[J] among these designs. If instead |dk−d~k|≤γ|d_{k}-\tilde{d}_{k}|\leq\gamma for some non-negative, non-increasing sequence d~\tilde{d}, LB is within 2​B​γ2B\gamma of the optimum.

By linearity, 𝔼⁡[J]\mathbb{E}[J] falls by dkd_{k} for each label spent on a kk-pass group, so the problem is a fractional knapsack, and LB spends labels in decreasing order of dkd_{k}. Any fixed correction c≤ac\leq a gives dk≥0d_{k}\geq 0 (Proposition 5). The theorem compares whole-group designs that select by pass count alone and give caught hacks a fixed correction. Designs that read the prompts or the responses, audit part of a group, or rescale an audited group’s correction fall outside this class; the group-level advantage correction of Sakib et al. (2026) rescales and matches a full audit in expectation at any positive budget (Proposition 8). With centered advantages and exchangeable compositions, the conclusion extends to all designs that use only the pass counts, including per-item and partial audits (Theorem 2); with std normalization it does not (Appendix F). The monotonicity condition holds in a simple model.

Proposition 2 (Pure groups).

Suppose that, for every kk, the weak passes of a kk-pass group are all hacks with probability ρk\rho_{k} and all correct otherwise, other responses have reward bb, advantages use the unbiased group std with ϵ=0\epsilon=0, and caught hacks receive 2​b−a2b-a. Then dK=0d_{K}=0 and, for 1≤k<K1\leq k<K,

dk=2​ρk​(K−1)​(K−k)K3​k,d_{k}=2\rho_{k}\sqrt{\frac{(K-1)(K-k)}{K^{3}\,k}}, (2)

which is non-increasing in kk whenever ρk\rho_{k} is.

The factor (K−k)/k\sqrt{(K-k)/k} is proportional to the advantage of a weak pass among kk passes (Figure 2a): a hack that shares its group with few other passes is reinforced the most, and a label that reverses it buys the most. On 72 frozen-state panels from both environments, where groups mix hacks and correct answers and, with malformed responses, a pass’s advantage need not fall with kk, LB attained the optimum over the designs of Theorem 1 in 123 of the 144 cases (each panel scored by two objectives) and came within 4.2×10−44.2\times 10^{-4} of it in the rest (Appendix B). Designs that audit only part of a group can do better on these objectives, but such a design did worse than LB in real training (Section 5.4).

3.4 Unbiased per-item corrections under group std normalization

Without std normalization, Lemma 1 makes the raw gradient of reward-level per-item IPW equal in expectation to that of a full audit. With std normalization it is not, because the reward correction (c−a)/p(c-a)/p is large and lands on a single response before normalization.

Proposition 3 (Saturation).

Fix a group in which exactly one response receives reward RR and the other K−1K-1 rewards lie in [0,a][0,a]. As R→−∞R\to-\infty, the std-normalized advantage of that response tends to −(K−1)/K-(K-1)/\sqrt{K} and every other advantage tends to +1/K+1/\sqrt{K}.

A normalized advantage never falls below −(K−1)/K-(K-1)/\sqrt{K} (Lemma 2), so under IPW with small pp a caught hack receives a bounded negative advantage, whatever the size of the correction, while every other response in its group, including uncaught hacks, receives nearly the same positive advantage. In a Countdown-Code group with four hacks and four failures at our budget, the expected hack mass under IPW is +0.016+0.016, against −0.468-0.468 under a full audit and +0.468+0.468 without one, and as p→0p\to 0 it tends to the unaudited value (Proposition 7). Rescaling the post-normalization advantage change of a whole audited group by 1/qg1/q_{g}, by contrast, stays unbiased (Proposition 8).

4 Experimental setup

LeetCode (Qwen3-4B, LoRA).

We use the training code and data of Wong et al. (2026), built on verl (Sheng et al., 2024). Each prompt is a programming problem; the weak verifier runs either the problem’s tests or a run_tests function supplied by the response, and a hack passes the weak verifier but fails the problem’s real test suite, which serves as the strong verifier. We keep their batch shape and model (16 prompts with 16 responses per step, LoRA of rank 32 on Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025), group std normalization) and use a constant learning rate of 1.75×10−51.75\times 10^{-5}, because pilot arms with a larger rate became unstable within 40 steps (Table 1). All arms start from the step-80 adapter of an unaudited run, where 24.2% of training rollouts are hacks, and train for 40 steps with a fresh optimizer state. The budget is p=0.33p=0.33 of the weak passes and the reflected penalty is 2​b−a=−2.52b-a=-2.5.

Countdown-Code (Qwen2.5-3B, full fine-tuning).

In Countdown-Code (Khalifa et al., 2026) the model writes a solution file with an arithmetic expression and the target, and a test file; the weak reward is 1.2 if the test passes, 0.2 for well-formed output and 0 otherwise. The dominant hack replaces the target in the solution file by the value of an expression that uses the given numbers; the strong verifier checks the expression literal against the original numbers and target. We train Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024) with full-parameter GRPO in TRL (von Werra et al., 2020), matching the original settings (32 prompts with 8 responses per step, 2048-token limit, no KL term; Table 1). All arms start from step 32 of an unaudited run (25.4% hacks at the first step) and train for 40 steps. The budget is p=0.28p=0.28 and the reflected penalty is 2​b−a=−0.82b-a=-0.8.

Protocol.

Each comparison’s arms, primary metric and decision rule were committed before its runs started. Arms of a comparison share the seed and therefore the prompts at every step, and we report paired bootstrap 95% intervals over (step, prompt) units. The two main comparisons (LB against RB in LeetCode and against IPW in Countdown-Code) have three seeds each, with a seed-level tt-test; so do per-item random audits and the full-audit penalty comparison in LeetCode and LB without std normalization in Countdown-Code. The remaining comparisons use one seed. Final checkpoints are evaluated on 1000 Countdown-Code test problems with 8 samples each and on the 119 medium and hard LeetCode test problems of Wong et al. (2026) with 32 samples each. Further baselines (PAC, an oracle selection rule and audited-only learning) are described in Appendix C.

5 Predicting training from the frozen push

The analysis of Section 3 characterizes the expected update at a frozen policy state. This section tests how well that frozen push, the hack mass JJ, predicts training: which selections and correction values suppress hacking (Sections 5.1 and 5.2), how the outcome shifts with the budget, the penalty size and the audit unit (Section 5.3), and how often the sign of JJ at the starting state predicted a run and where it broke down (Section 5.4).

Differences are first arm minus second, in percentage points, with paired bootstrap 95% intervals over (step, prompt) units in training and over problems on held-out panels. These intervals capture variation within a pair of runs; variation across seeds enters through the three-seed comparisons and the seed-level tests. Figure 3 summarizes the main paired comparisons, per-seed tables are in Appendix D, and seed-level tests in Appendix J.

5.1 Under the reflected penalty, which groups are audited decides the outcome

LB and RB use the same penalty and audit whole groups until a third of the weak passes are checked; only the order of the groups differs. In LeetCode, LB removes hacking within about ten steps in all three seeds, while RB lets it rise from about a quarter of rollouts to 36.33–51.68% in the last ten steps, close to the unaudited run (53.40%; Figure 1b). Auditing single weak passes at random with the same penalty and budget fails as well, with late hacking of 45.62–55.78%. The area under the hacking curve is 30.89–41.53 points lower for LB than for RB, and 40.31–41.25 points lower than for random items (Figure 3a). Late correctness shows no detectable difference between LB and RB (Figure 5 in Appendix D). Because the budget is a fraction of the weak passes, LB’s spending falls as hacking is suppressed: it used 53% of RB’s labels and 51% of those of random items (Figure 1c).

The difference starts with what each label finds. In the first five steps, when the arms are in similar states, each LB label caught a hack 62.5%, 55.4% and 56.5% of the time, against 45.9%, 45.5% and 43.9% for RB. On held-out problems, RB’s hacking generalizes in all three seeds, at 50.8%, 62.2% and 49.1% of responses against 0.3%, 0.1% and 0.1% for LB (14.9% at the starting checkpoint), while held-out accuracy shows no detectable difference (Figure 3b).

In Countdown-Code, one seed of random whole-group audits with the same penalty and budget rule also failed to suppress hacking: late hacking was 50.12% against 0.08% for LB, and the area under the hacking curve was 33.51 points higher [++31.50, ++35.40]. Because hacking spread, it used 69% more labels than LB. On held-out problems its hacking persisted (48.8% of responses) and LB answered 5.3 points more problems correctly [++3.9, ++6.7].

Strict hacking understates the difference in behavior: a LeetCode response can pass the real tests while defining its own run_tests, and such responses carry the behavior that produces hacks (Wong et al., 2026). In the last ten steps, 0.12–0.39% of LB’s responses define their own tests, against 83.67–94.53% for RB (Appendix G).

5.2 The correction value decides whether targeting helps

Holding the selection fixed (Table 5), auditing the 8 lowest-pass groups per step with the strong-verdict reward c=bc=b leaves late hacking at 46.37%, no better than auditing 8 random groups (42.46%), whereas with the reflected penalty the same 8 groups remove hacking (0.04%), with 4.96 points higher late correctness and 53% of the labels; they also beat a single-seed pilot that audited every weak pass with c=bc=b (3.12% late hacking) at 34% of its labels. With c=bc=b, a fully caught all-hack group contributes no update, while hacks in the many unaudited high-pass groups are still reinforced (Proposition 1). In three later seeds of full coverage, c=bc=b left late strict hacking at 21.09%, 1.37% and 8.36% and late attempts at 43.01%, 1.80% and 15.08%, whereas the reflected penalty removed strict hacking and drove attempts to at most 0.12% (Appendix G).

5.3 Budget, penalty size and audit unit

Low budgets.

At a budget of 0.1 of the weak passes, LB did not suppress hacking in LeetCode (late hacking 40.2% and 45.0% in two seeds), while at 0.2 it did (0.12% and 0.27%) with 61–63% of the labels of LB at 0.33. At 0.1 the audited groups are too few for their corrections to outweigh the reinforcement of the unaudited hacks. Multiplying the change in the audited groups’ normalized advantages by 3.1 (the frozen-panel ratio of the full audit’s change in hack mass to LB’s; a design outside Theorem 1) suppressed hacking (0.04%), with no detectable difference from LB at 0.33 in the area under the hacking curve (+0.33−0.47+0.48+0.33^{+0.48}_{-0.47}) and 33% of its labels. The group-level advantage correction at 0.1 also suppressed hacking (0.82%), slightly more slowly (one seed each). A heavier penalty (−11.5-11.5) at 0.1 suppressed hacking only for a while: from 2.0% around steps 16–20 it rose to 10.2% in steps 36–40, and to 44.9% within ten steps of a continuation with a fresh optimizer.

The audit unit under std normalization.

Lemma 1 assumes centered advantages. With std normalization, LeetCode runs at equal marginals went both ways: with penalty 0 whole groups had slightly lower hacking than independent items (three seeds), and with a heavy penalty of −11.5-11.5 items suppressed hacking and whole groups did not (two seeds). An exact condition for one group explains both (Appendix F).

5.4 Predictions from the starting state, and where the push stops predicting

Predictions from the starting state.

For each run, we computed the hack mass JJ of its design on a frozen panel of about 1000 prompts at its starting checkpoint and predicted from its sign whether hacking would be suppressed (late hacking below 2%) or persist (10% or more). Over the 39 runs whose designs we scored this way, 33 predictions held. For 16 runs the prediction was committed before the run started (Appendix I), and 13 of these held, in both directions: LB failed at a budget of 0.1 and succeeded at 0.2 in two seeds each, LB with corrections scaled by 3.1 and the group-level advantage correction succeeded at 0.1, and random group audits failed in Countdown-Code. The other three ended between the two thresholds and nearer the predicted side: 2.19% and 3.44% late hacking for two runs predicted to suppress hacking (seed 1 of the Countdown-Code group-level correction and seed 2 of the LeetCode one), and 7.9% for one predicted not to (LB with penalty −11.5-11.5 at 0.1, which suppressed hacking for about 15 steps before it rose); a continuation of that run, preregistered with separate thresholds, rose to 40.5% against a frozen-sign prediction of below 10%. Of the other 23 runs, the sign matched all 13 LeetCode runs of the main comparison and its references (LB, random group audits and random item audits in three seeds each, no audit, and the full audit in three seeds) and all six Countdown-Code runs of LB and the full audit, but it missed three of the four audit-unit runs at penalty −11.5-11.5 and p=0.4p=0.4 (Appendix F): whole-group audits (J=−0.002J=-0.002) did not suppress hacking in either seed, and per-item audits (J=−0.067J=-0.067) did in one seed but rose to 13.7% in the other. Designs we did not score on the starting panels (the strong-verdict arms, the audit-unit runs at penalty 0, the per-item IPW variants and LB without std normalization) are not included. Within these two environments and related designs, the sign of the frozen push anticipated the outcome in most runs.

Light penalties and widespread hacking.

LB’s ordering assumes that low-pass groups hold a large share of the hacks. In the LeetCode runs with c=bc=b, hacking spread, and the share of hacks in groups with at least 12 of 16 weak passes rose from about half to over 80%; the 8 lowest-pass groups then held no more hacks than random groups. Under the reflected penalty hacking collapsed within the first ten steps, before it could spread to high-pass groups.

An online rule that optimizes the frozen objective.

Auditing part of each group, with the number of labels chosen from the estimated composition of groups with each pass count, improves JJ beyond LB on frozen panels. In a preregistered LeetCode pilot from step 120 (p=0.2p=0.2), such a rule was worse than LB: its area under the hacking curve was 4.90 points higher and its late hacking 47.81% against 31.25%, although its realized JJ was more negative in every phase. So JJ is not the first-order change in the hacking rate, which also depends on the directions of all responses’ gradients and on the optimizer. A one-step diagnosis did not identify the cause, but showed that which of several similar hacks in a partially audited group receives the penalty is a large source of noise in a single update, which whole-group audits do not have (Appendix H).

6 Beyond the expected update: unbiased corrections

Unbiased corrections target the full audit’s update: on a frozen batch, per-item reward-level IPW without std normalization has the full audit’s expected update by Lemma 1, and so does the group-level advantage correction of Sakib et al. (2026) by Proposition 8. Comparing the group-level correction with LB and with a full audit therefore separates the expected update from the randomness of its estimate and the allocation of audits.

Per-item reward-level IPW targets the same reflected reward as LB in Countdown-Code, spends about the same number of labels, and, following Lemma 1, runs without std normalization. Both suppress hacking, with late hacking below 1% in every run, but LB ends with higher late correctness in all three seeds, by 4.53–11.13 points, and answers more held-out problems correctly, by 6.1–11.8 points (Figures 4 and 3). Part of the held-out gap comes from unfinished answers: IPW left 3.3–13.9% of its answers cut at the 2048-token limit, against 0.2–1.6% for LB. Among parseable answers LB was still more accurate in every seed, by 4.5–5.9 points, with each interval above zero; comparisons among parseable answers condition on an answer being finished, so the subsets compared need not have the same difficulty. Continuing every cut answer to 4096 tokens from its own prefix made only 9 of 1779 correct, and LB’s lead was unchanged at 6.1–11.7 points. The correction value matters for IPW too: targeting c=bc=b instead of −0.8-0.8 leaves late hacking at 14.73%, and adding group std normalization, which breaks its unbiasedness (Section 3.4), leaves it at 19.06% (single seeds; Table 5).

Group-level advantage correction.

Sakib et al. (2026) correct the advantages instead of the rewards: an audited group’s normalized advantages move from their weak-reward values toward their full-audit values by the change divided by the audit probability, which matches a full audit in expectation (Proposition 8). In LeetCode, auditing each group with probability 0.33 (the expected budget of LB) suppressed hacking in two of three seeds, slightly faster than LB, and left late hacking at 3.44% in the third; held-out accuracy showed no detectable difference from LB in any seed (Figure 3), although in LeetCode held-out accuracy barely moved even under widespread hacking (Section 5.1), so this comparison has little power. In Countdown-Code at p=0.28p=0.28 it also brought hacking down (late hacking 0.35–2.19%, the highest just above our 2% threshold for suppression), but in all three seeds it ended with lower late training correctness, by 3.48–9.92 points, and LB answered more held-out problems correctly, by 8.0–11.5 points, each interval above zero (Figures 4 and 3). In seed 1, 23.4% of the correction’s held-out answers were unparseable, almost all cut at the length limit, and among parseable answers it was more accurate than LB, but continuing the cut answers to 4096 tokens made only 7 of 1863 correct and left the gap at 7.9 points [++6.6, ++9.2]; in seeds 2 and 3 few answers were unparseable (3.8% and 0.3%), and LB was more accurate among parseable answers as well, by 10.0–10.9 points. Its late response length varied widely across seeds (677–1117 tokens, against 749–847 for LB; Figure 4) while its accuracy loss did not, so length growth alone cannot explain the accuracy loss across the three seeds.

Two preregistered controls locate the gap. On a common frozen batch, every unbiased group-level design has the full audit’s advantages, and hence its raw first-order policy gradient, as its expectation. A full audit with the reflected penalty stayed within about two points of LB on held-out problems in all three seeds, with LB minus the full audit at −-2.1 [−-3.6, −-0.7], 0.0 [−-1.3, ++1.2] and ++2.2 [++1.0, ++3.4], far from the uniform correction’s gap, so the correction does not lose by aiming at the full-audit update. Allocating the same correction by pass count, with audit probabilities that fall with the number of weak passes (weights chosen to reduce the variance of the corrected advantages on a frozen panel of 1000 groups whose 5250 weak passes were all checked by the strong verifier, labels not counted in its training budget of 1498; floor 0.1), recovered most of the gap at the same expected budget: its held-out accuracy was 6.8 points above the uniform correction’s [++5.4, ++8.1] and 1.2 points below LB’s [−-0.1, ++2.5] (one seed). The loss therefore comes not from the full-audit update that the correction estimates but from the randomness of the estimate and how the audits behind it are allocated; which part of that randomness hurts we have not identified. At this budget LB accepts a bias in the update for low noise, and its held-out accuracy stayed within about two points of a full audit’s with 28% of its labels.

LB without std normalization.

LB does not depend on std normalization. In Countdown-Code over three seeds, LB without it also suppressed hacking and ended with higher late correctness than LB with it, by 4.45–11.05 points, at the cost of longer responses and more labels (Appendix E).

7 Related work

Reward hacking under verifiable rewards.

Checks that a policy can satisfy without solving the task are a recurring failure of RLVR. Countdown-Code isolates the phenomenon in a small code environment (Khalifa et al., 2026); ImpossibleBench measures the propensity of models to exploit tests (Zhong et al., 2025); patches counted as solved on SWE-bench fail the repository’s full suite (Wang et al., 2025); and systematic verifier errors can delay or derail RLVR (Egashira et al., 2026). Optimizing against a monitor of reasoning teaches the policy to hide its intent (Baker et al., 2025), a training-time instance of reward-model overoptimization (Gao et al., 2022), and Deng et al. (2026) predict when detectable hacking will emerge.

Interventions during training.

Wong et al. (2026) benchmark monitor-based penalties and screening in the LeetCode environment we use and observe that correct responses that also attempt the hack keep the behavior alive (Appendix G). HackFree-GRPO (Anonymous, 2026) discounts and filters trajectories scored by a frozen detector under centered advantages and shows that a discounted hack can keep a positive advantage; it scores every trajectory and has no strong-verifier budget to allocate. GRAFT (Ward et al., 2026) routes the gradients of flagged samples into parameters removed after training. Moya et al. (2026) show that partial audits suffice when the correction outweighs the pressure toward hacking and propose PAC, a projected gradient correction we compare against in adapted form; their audits are independent per item.

Budgeted audits and labels.

AI Control spends a scarce budget of trusted audits on the most suspicious outputs at deployment (Greenblatt et al., 2023). CARE acquires ground-truth labels where the gap between pseudo-label and true-label advantages is largest (Wang et al., 2026); our oracle selection uses this criterion with true labels. Selecting the hardest examples for GRPO under an annotation budget works best (Pikus et al., 2025); LB applies a related preference for low-pass groups online. PAIR applies Horvitz–Thompson reweighting to adaptive rollout allocation and notes that dividing by a random group standard deviation biases ratio estimators (Nomand et al., 2026). Sakib et al. (2026) quantify, without training, the variance of whole-group and per-attempt random audits with reward-level and advantage-level inverse-propensity corrections for coding agents (Section 1).

Group normalization and correlated errors.

Dr. GRPO removes std normalization from GRPO (Liu et al., 2025). Gupta (2026) shows that changing only the correlation of rewards within a group can reverse the expected group-normalized update, and Xin (2026) measure correlated verifier errors within groups. STAR-GRPO down-weights unreliable ratings before normalization (Tian et al., 2026), and noise-corrected GRPO corrects exogenous reward noise in expectation (El Mansouri et al., 2025). Lemma 1 is the centered-advantage counterpart of these observations for audits, and Proposition 3 makes explicit how std normalization defeats unbiased per-item corrections.

8 Conclusion and limitations

Conclusion.

A small strong-verifier budget can suppress reward hacking in GRPO, provided it is spent where uncaught hacks gain the most and caught hacks are pushed away rather than merely zeroed. At a frozen state, auditing whole groups with the fewest weak passes first minimizes the advantage mass left on hacks among whole-group pass-count designs with a fixed correction, when a label’s value does not increase with the pass count. From the starting state, the sign of this mass predicted whether hacking would be suppressed in 33 of 39 runs, including 13 of 16 preregistered ones. In our experiments the following recipe worked in both environments: give caught hacks the reflected reward 2​b−a2b-a; audit whole groups with the fewest weak passes first; set the budget as a fraction of weak passes, so that spending falls when weak passes fall as hacking is suppressed; and avoid per-item reward-level inverse-propensity corrections under group std normalization. Randomness matters as well. Unbiased corrections can match LB on hacking, but in Countdown-Code their randomness cost correctness at the same budget: a full audit stayed within about two points of LB, and reallocating the audits recovered most of the loss.

Limitations.

Our experiments cover two environments, 3B and 4B models, and 40-step windows that start after hacking has emerged; we have not tested whether hacking returns over longer training or at larger scale. In both environments the strong verifier is cheap enough that the budget is a design choice rather than a necessity; we have not tested a setting where the strong verifier is itself expensive or imperfect. We treat the strong verifier as reliable and independent of the policy, and a strong verifier with blind spots would push the policy toward them, as observed for optimized monitors (Baker et al., 2025; Ward et al., 2026). The two main comparisons and several ablations have three seeds; the group-level advantage correction has three seeds in each environment and the full audit three in Countdown-Code, and other comparisons, including the allocated correction, have one or two. The correctness advantage of LB over per-item IPW is positive in all three seeds, with p=0.055p=0.055 in training and p=0.040p=0.040 on held-out problems at the seed level, and against the group-level correction it is positive in all three seeds, among parseable answers in two of them. Our decision metrics, hacking and correctness on training rollouts, missed length drift, which appeared in rollout lengths and on held-out panels. Our analysis is first order at a frozen state: the sign of its objective predicted whether hacking would be suppressed in 33 of 39 runs (13 of 16 preregistered), but its magnitude does not rank designs, as the online rule showed. These predictions come from two environments and related designs and have not been compared with a simple baseline. The reflected penalty is exact only when non-passing responses share the reward bb.

All random objects take finitely many values. Token-mean aggregation weights each response’s score by quantities that depend on response lengths, not on rewards, so the weights are fixed given the batch and are absorbed into ∇θ​log​πθ​(yi∣xi)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x_{i}). If 2​b−a≤02b-a\leq 0, the reward 2​b−a2b-a is the smallest possible reward, so a caught hack has a non-positive advantage in any group. ∎

Appendix B Further theoretical results

These results support remarks in Section 3; the same setting and conventions apply.

Lemma 2 (A bound on normalized advantages).

For every group reward vector rr with σ⁡(r)>0\sigma(r)>0, every ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0 and every ii, the normalized advantage satisfies |Ai|≤(K−1)/K|A_{i}|\leq(K-1)/\sqrt{K}.

Proof.

Let ej=rj−r¯e_{j}=r_{j}-\bar{r}, so that ∑jej=0\sum_{j}e_{j}=0 and ∑jej2=(K−1)​σ2\sum_{j}e_{j}^{2}=(K-1)\sigma^{2}. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality over j≠ij\neq i, ei2=(∑j≠iej)2≤(K−1)​((K−1)​σ2−ei2)e_{i}^{2}=\big(\sum_{j\neq i}e_{j}\big)^{2}\leq(K-1)\big((K-1)\sigma^{2}-e_{i}^{2}\big), so |ei|≤σ⁡(K−1)/K|e_{i}|\leq\sigma(K-1)/\sqrt{K}. Divide by σ+ϵ≥σ\sigma+\epsilon\geq\sigma. ∎

Proposition 4 (Group-adaptive reflection).

Let a group contain hh hacks, 1≤h≤K−11\leq h\leq K-1, all audited, and let μN\mu_{N} be the mean reward of its N=K−hN=K-h other responses. If every hack receives 2​μN−a2\mu_{N}-a and Δ=2​h​(a−μN)/K\Delta=2h(a-\mu_{N})/K, then each hack’s deviation from the group mean is negated, each other response’s deviation increases by Δ\Delta, and the group’s standard deviation is unchanged. Hence every hack’s advantage is negated, for both advantage forms, and the advantages of the other responses all shift by the same amount (Δ\Delta centered; Δ/(σ+ϵ)\Delta/(\sigma+\epsilon) normalized, or 00 if σ=ϵ=0\sigma=\epsilon=0), so their contrasts are unchanged.

Proof.

The weak mean is r¯=(h​a+N​μN)/K\bar{r}=(ha+N\mu_{N})/K, so r¯−μN=Δ/2\bar{r}-\mu_{N}=\Delta/2, and the new mean is r¯−Δ\bar{r}-\Delta. A hack’s new deviation is (2​μN−a)−r¯+Δ=−(a−r¯)(2\mu_{N}-a)-\bar{r}+\Delta=-(a-\bar{r}) because 2​(r¯−μN)=Δ2(\bar{r}-\mu_{N})=\Delta. The other responses keep their rewards while the mean falls by Δ\Delta. With eje_{j} their old deviations, ∑j(ej+Δ)2=∑jej2+2​Δ​∑jej+N​Δ2\sum_{j}(e_{j}+\Delta)^{2}=\sum_{j}e_{j}^{2}+2\Delta\sum_{j}e_{j}+N\Delta^{2}, and ∑jej=N(μN−r¯)=−NΔ/2\sum_{j}e_{j}=N(\mu_{N}-\bar{r})=-N\Delta/2, so the sum of squared deviations is unchanged. ∎

This correction needs the strong labels of every weak pass of the group and can be computed only after all of them have been audited. When the other responses all have reward bb, it equals 2​b−a2b-a (Proposition 1).

Proposition 5 (Lowering the hack reward never raises the hack mass).

Fix a group with hh hacks, 1≤h≤K−11\leq h\leq K-1, whose hacks share a common reward tt while the other rewards are fixed. For centered advantages, and for normalized advantages with any ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, the group’s hack mass Φ⁡(t)=1K​∑i∈HAi\Phi(t)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i\in H}A_{i} is non-decreasing in tt. Consequently a whole-group audit with any fixed correction c≤ac\leq a does not raise the hack mass of any group, and dk≥0d_{k}\geq 0 for every kk.

With N=K−hN=K-h, μN\mu_{N} and SNS_{N} the mean and sum of squared deviations of the other rewards, and x=t−μNx=t-\mu_{N}, each hack deviates from the mean by N​x/KNx/K and the sum of squared deviations is SN+h​N​x2/KS_{N}+hNx^{2}/K. The centered hack mass is h​N​x/K2hNx/K^{2}. The normalized one is (h​N/K2)​x/(γ′+β​x2+ϵ)(hN/K^{2})\,x/(\sqrt{\gamma^{\prime}+\beta x^{2}}+\epsilon) with γ′=SN/(K−1)≥0\gamma^{\prime}=S_{N}/(K-1)\geq 0 and β=h​N/(K⁡(K−1))>0\beta=hN/(K(K-1))>0, whose derivative in xx is (γ′/γ′+β​x2+ϵ)/(γ′+β​x2+ϵ)2≥0\big(\gamma^{\prime}/\sqrt{\gamma^{\prime}+\beta x^{2}}+\epsilon\big)/\big(\sqrt{\gamma^{\prime}+\beta x^{2}}+\epsilon\big)^{2}\geq 0 where γ′+β​x2>0\gamma^{\prime}+\beta x^{2}>0; if γ′=0\gamma^{\prime}=0 the function is x/(β​|x|+ϵ)x/(\sqrt{\beta}|x|+\epsilon) with value 00 at x=0x=0, which is also non-decreasing. A whole-group audit lowers the common hack reward from aa to c≤ac\leq a. ∎

Remark 1 (Other group-separable objectives).

The proof of Theorem 1 uses only that the objective is a sum over groups of a quantity determined by each group’s composition and audit decision. It therefore holds for any such objective, for example JJ minus the advantage mass on correct responses, with dkd_{k} defined from that objective.

Proposition 6 (Centered advantages).

With centered advantages and a fixed correction c<ac<a, a full audit lowers the hack mass of any group with hh hacks by (a−c)​h​(K−h)/K2(a-c)h(K-h)/K^{2}, whatever its other responses. Hence dk=(a−c)​𝔼​[h⁡(K−h)∣k]/(k​K2)≥0d_{k}=(a-c)\,\mathbb{E}[h(K-h)\mid k]/(kK^{2})\geq 0. If each pass of a kk-pass group is a hack independently with probability η∈(0,1]\eta\in(0,1], then dk=(a−c)​η​(K−1+η−k​η)/K2d_{k}=(a-c)\eta(K-1+\eta-k\eta)/K^{2}, which strictly decreases in kk, also for groups that mix hacks and correct answers.

A full audit lowers each hack’s reward by a−ca-c and the group mean by h⁡(a−c)/Kh(a-c)/K, so each hack’s centered advantage falls by (a−c)​(1−h/K)(a-c)(1-h/K); sum over the hh hacks and divide by KK. In the binomial model 𝔼⁡[h⁡(K−h)]=K​k​η−k​η​(1−η)−k2​η2\mathbb{E}[h(K-h)]=Kk\eta-k\eta(1-\eta)-k^{2}\eta^{2}. ∎

Theorem 2 (LB among all pass-count designs, centered advantages).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1, suppose in addition that, given the number of hacks in a group, every set of its passes of that size is equally likely to be the hacks. With centered advantages and a fixed correction c<ac<a, consider any design with this correction (per-item, whole-group or partial) whose audit law depends only on the pass counts and on independent randomness, and let ygy_{g} be its expected labels on group gg. Then 𝔼[J]=∑gμkg0−∑g:kg≥1ygdkg\mathbb{E}[J]=\sum_{g}\mu^{0}_{k_{g}}-\sum_{g:\,k_{g}\geq 1}y_{g}d_{k_{g}} with dkd_{k} from Proposition 6, so if dkd_{k} is non-increasing, LB minimizes 𝔼⁡[J]\mathbb{E}[J] over all such designs.

Proof.

For a fixed composition with hack set HgH_{g} of size hh, catching hack ii (probability πi\pi_{i}) lowers the group’s hack mass by (a−c)​(1−h/K)/K(a-c)(1-h/K)/K by linearity, so the expected hack mass is Φg​(0)−(a−c)​(1−h/K)​K−1​∑i∈Hgπi\Phi_{g}(0)-(a-c)(1-h/K)K^{-1}\sum_{i\in H_{g}}\pi_{i}. The marginals do not depend on the composition, and by exchangeability 𝔼⁡[∑i∈Hgπi∣h]=(h/kg)​yg\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i\in H_{g}}\pi_{i}\mid h]=(h/k_{g})y_{g}. Taking expectations gives 𝔼⁡[Φg]=μkg0−yg​dkg\mathbb{E}[\Phi_{g}]=\mu^{0}_{k_{g}}-y_{g}d_{k_{g}}, which has the form used in the proof of Theorem 1. ∎

With std normalization the conclusion fails: in the group of Appendix F, per-item audits at the same marginals lower the hack mass more than a whole-group audit when the penalty is heavy.

Proposition 7 (Per-item reward-level IPW at small rates).

Fix a group with h≥1h\geq 1 hacks, normalized advantages with ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, and independent per-item audits with probability pp in which a caught hack receives any reward (possibly depending on pp). Let Φw\Phi_{w} be the group’s hack mass without an audit and CK,h=h⁡(K−h)​(K−1)/K3C_{K,h}=\sqrt{h(K-h)(K-1)/K^{3}}. Then |𝔼⁡[Φp]−Φw|≤2​CK,h​(1−(1−p)h)≤2​CK,h​h​p|\mathbb{E}[\Phi_{p}]-\Phi_{w}|\leq 2C_{K,h}(1-(1-p)^{h})\leq 2C_{K,h}hp, so the expected hack mass tends to its unaudited value as p→0p\to 0.

Proof.

Since the normalized advantages sum to zero, Φ=1K∑iAi(𝟏[i∈H]−h/K)\Phi=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i}A_{i}(\mathbf{1}[i\in H]-h/K), and by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality |Φ|≤1K​K−1​h⁡(K−h)/K=CK,h|\Phi|\leq\frac{1}{K}\sqrt{K-1}\sqrt{h(K-h)/K}=C_{K,h}, using ∑iAi2≤K−1\sum_{i}A_{i}^{2}\leq K-1. If no hack is caught, which has probability (1−p)h(1-p)^{h}, the rewards equal the weak rewards and Φp=Φw\Phi_{p}=\Phi_{w}; otherwise |Φp−Φw|≤2​CK,h|\Phi_{p}-\Phi_{w}|\leq 2C_{K,h}. ∎

Proposition 3 does not imply that IPW with std normalization fails in general: with K=2K=2, one hack and one failure at bb, a target c<bc<b and ϵ=0\epsilon=0, the hack’s advantage is +1/2+1/\sqrt{2} when it is not caught and −1/2-1/\sqrt{2} when it is, so its expected advantage (1−2​p)/2(1-2p)/\sqrt{2} is negative for p>1/2p>1/2.

Proposition 8 (Group-level advantage correction).

For each group let Zg∼Bernoulli⁡(qg)Z_{g}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q_{g}) with qg∈(0,1]q_{g}\in(0,1] fixed given the batch, let rFr^{F} be the rewards after a full audit with correction cc, and set A^i=Ai​(rw)+(Zg/qg)​(Ai​(rF)−Ai​(rw))\hat{A}_{i}=A_{i}(r^{w})+(Z_{g}/q_{g})(A_{i}(r^{F})-A_{i}(r^{w})) for ii in group gg, for either advantage form. Then 𝔼⁡[A^i]=Ai​(rF)\mathbb{E}[\hat{A}_{i}]=A_{i}(r^{F}), so the expected update equals that of a full audit; Var⁡(A^i)=1−qgqg​(Ai​(rF)−Ai​(rw))2\mathrm{Var}(\hat{A}_{i})=\frac{1-q_{g}}{q_{g}}(A_{i}(r^{F})-A_{i}(r^{w}))^{2}; the expected number of labels is ∑gqg​kg\sum_{g}q_{g}k_{g}; and ∑i∈gA^i=0\sum_{i\in g}\hat{A}_{i}=0.

Proof.

𝔼⁡[Zg/qg]=1\mathbb{E}[Z_{g}/q_{g}]=1 and Var⁡(Zg/qg)=(1−qg)/qg\mathrm{Var}(Z_{g}/q_{g})=(1-q_{g})/q_{g}, and A^i\hat{A}_{i} is affine in Zg/qgZ_{g}/q_{g}; both advantage vectors sum to zero within the group. ∎

In our implementation the advantages are normalized before the correction and the trainer’s own normalization is switched off: normalizing A^\hat{A} again would be nonlinear in ZgZ_{g} and would destroy unbiasedness, whereas the trainer’s group centering leaves A^\hat{A} unchanged. The design generally falls outside the class of Theorem 1, because the update applied to an audited group is the full-audit change multiplied by 1/qg1/q_{g}.

A worked example of saturation.

At the Countdown-Code budget (K=8K=8, p=0.28p=0.28, so a caught hack receives R=1.2+(−0.8−1.2)/0.28≈−5.94R=1.2+(-0.8-1.2)/0.28\approx-5.94), a group with four hacks of which one is caught and four failures at 0.20.2 gives the caught hack a normalized advantage of −2.42-2.42, the uncaught hacks +0.59+0.59 and the failures +0.17+0.17; the limits of Proposition 3 are −2.47-2.47 and +0.35+0.35. A whole-group audit of this group gives the hacks −0.94-0.94 and the failures +0.94+0.94 (Proposition 1). Averaged over the binomial number of caught hacks, the group’s expected hack mass is +0.016+0.016 under IPW, −0.468-0.468 under a full audit and +0.468+0.468 without an audit; with centered advantages IPW and the full audit agree at −0.25-0.25. This compares IPW with the full audit, not with LB at the same budget: auditing this one group as a whole with probability 0.280.28 gives +0.206+0.206.

Frozen-panel check of the monotonicity condition.

We checked the condition of Theorem 1 on frozen-state panels of about 1000 prompts each: 48 Countdown-Code combinations (steps 12–32 of an unaudited run, penalty −0.8-0.8 or −3.8-3.8, audit rate 0.1–0.4) and 24 LeetCode combinations (steps 70, 80 and 120; penalty −2.5-2.5 or −11.5-11.5; rate 0.1–0.4). Each was scored by JJ alone and by JJ minus the advantage mass on correct responses (Remark 1). With the panels’ empirical label values, LB attained the optimum over the designs of Theorem 1 in 123 of the 144 cases and was within 4.2×10−44.2\times 10^{-4} of it in the rest.

Appendix C Experimental details

Strong verifiers.

In LeetCode, a response is a hack when it passes the weak verifier only through its own run_tests function and fails the problem’s tests; responses that pass the problem’s tests are correct even if they also define run_tests. In Countdown-Code, a weak pass is a hack when its expression literal does not use exactly the given numbers or does not evaluate to the given target.

Baselines.

In Countdown-Code we also compare against three alternatives. PAC (Moya et al., 2026) keeps the weak reward and adds a correction along an inverse-propensity estimate of the hack-probability gradient, projected to be orthogonal to the reward gradient. The original Euclidean rule collapsed the policy within one step under full-parameter training, so we use an adaptation in which the projection is taken in the metric of AdamW’s diagonal preconditioner after the batch’s optimizer updates; the guarantees of the original method, stated for a fixed metric and gradient flow, do not carry over. The correction size was selected on a separate development state. An oracle selection rule (Cag) reads the semantic labels and audits groups in decreasing order of the corrective advantage gap, the acquisition criterion of CARE (Wang et al., 2026), under LB’s budget; it is not the full CARE method. Audited-only learning (Ao) uses LB’s audits but drops unaudited groups from the update.

Held-out panels and protocol.

Held-out evaluation uses the final checkpoints of all three seeds of the two main comparisons, seeds 2 and 3 of no-std LB, and the single-seed Countdown-Code arms: 1000 Countdown-Code test problems with 8 samples each, and the 119 medium and hard LeetCode test problems of Wong et al. (2026) with 32 samples each, plus 353 held-out training-split LeetCode problems with 16 samples each for the difficulty strata of Appendix G and the group-level correction. Paired bootstrap intervals use 4000 resamples over 640 (LeetCode) or 1280 (Countdown-Code) (step, prompt) units, or over problems.

Compute.

Training ran on two NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, one arm per GPU, at about two hours per 40-step arm. Held-out panels ran on separate RTX 3090 and A6000 GPUs.

Appendix D Per-seed results

In the tables, entries are estimates with the distances to the upper and lower ends of the 95% interval, x−l+ux^{+u}_{-l}.

Appendix E Group std normalization and other baselines in Countdown-Code

Adding group std normalization to IPW breaks its unbiasedness and, in our run, strongly attenuated its correction, consistent with Proposition 3: hacking plateaus at 19.06% instead of 0.82%. LB does not depend on std normalization, and in Countdown-Code it trained better without it. Over three seeds, LB without std normalization suppressed hacking as well (late hacking at most 0.12%) and ended with higher late correctness than LB with it in every seed, by 4.45–11.05 pp, with higher pass@8 in every seed. The cost is 5% to 11% more labels and 18% to 30% more generated tokens, because responses grow longer. On held-out problems, the no-std LB checkpoints of seeds 2 and 3 answer 54.6% and 54.2% correctly (2.2 and 2.0 pp above LB with std normalization, and 14.0 and 9.4 pp above IPW at the same seeds), with a truncation tradeoff: in seed 3, 18.7% of held-out responses were unparseable, almost all after reaching the 2048-token limit, compared with 0.2% for std-normalized LB. Removing std normalization changes GRPO’s weighting of easy and hard prompts (Liu et al., 2025); LB composes with it. When LB runs without std normalization, its late correctness exceeds that of IPW at the same seed by 17.03 and 12.19 pp in seeds 2 and 3, so the gap between LB and IPW is not an artifact of the normalization.

PAC (Moya et al., 2026) keeps the weak reward, so each GRPO step still reinforces hacks, and the projected correction is locally orthogonal to the weak-reward gradient in the chosen metric. With per-item audits at the same rate, hacking rose to 64.80% in the late window, and the unprojected correction reached 15.20% (Table 5). The oracle selection rule (Cag) matched LB on hacking and correctness, including held-out accuracy, with 648 labels against 1403, mainly because it skips groups whose corrective gap is zero. Learning only from audited groups (Ao) matched LB on hacking and correctness but drifted toward long responses (1148 against 749 tokens on average in the late window); 34.4% of its held-out responses gave no answer, almost all because they reached the 2048-token limit.

Appendix F The audit unit at equal marginals

The two experiments also differ in prompts per step and in how the number of audited groups is drawn, so they are not a strict two-factor design. Spreading heavy penalties over many groups saturates the normalized advantages of every group with a caught hack (Proposition 3), which also shrinks the positive advantage of the uncaught hacks beside it, whereas random whole-group audits leave the unaudited groups untouched. At penalty −2.5-2.5 and p=0.33p=0.33, per-item random audits also failed to suppress hacking, with an AUC difference against RB of ++10.36, −-1.22 and ++4.08 pp over the three seeds; we have not tested per-item low-pass targeting.

An exact comparison for one group.

Fix a group with kk weak passes, of which h≥1h\geq 1 are hacks and the rest correct, and failures at reward bb, and let Ψ⁡(j)\Psi(j) be its normalized hack mass 1K​∑i∈HAi\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i\in H}A_{i} when jj of the hh hacks are caught. Auditing the whole group with probability pp gives EG=(1−p)​Ψ​(0)+p​Ψ​(h)E_{G}=(1-p)\Psi(0)+p\Psi(h); auditing each weak pass independently with probability pp catches X∼Binomial⁡(h,p)X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(h,p) hacks and gives EI=∑j(hj)​pj​(1−p)h−j​Ψ​(j)E_{I}=\sum_{j}\binom{h}{j}p^{j}(1-p)^{h-j}\Psi(j), at the same expected cost. Since 𝔼⁡[X]=h​p\mathbb{E}[X]=hp,

EI−EG=∑j=1h−1Pr⁡(X=j)​[Ψ⁡(j)−(1−jh)​Ψ​(0)−jh​Ψ​(h)],E_{I}-E_{G}=\sum_{j=1}^{h-1}\Pr(X=j)\Big[\Psi(j)-\Big(1-\frac{j}{h}\Big)\Psi(0)-\frac{j}{h}\Psi(h)\Big],

so per-item audits lower the hack mass more than whole-group audits exactly when Ψ\Psi at intermediate depths lies, on average, below the chord between its end points; with centered advantages Ψ\Psi is affine in jj and the two agree. For K=16K=16, h=8h=8, k=10k=10, (a,b)=(3.5,0.5)(a,b)=(3.5,0.5) and p=0.4p=0.4, penalty 0 gives EG=0.1161E_{G}=0.1161 and EI=0.1316E_{I}=0.1316 (whole groups better), while penalty −11.5-11.5 gives EG=0.0333E_{G}=0.0333 and EI=−0.1494E_{I}=-0.1494 (single items better).

The D0 comparison was first run with 16 prompts per step and a random number of audited groups; its three seeds gave −4.18-4.18, −0.41-0.41 and +3.02+3.02 pp, too noisy to decide, and we preregistered the 32-prompt version above before running it. The seed-level mean of the 32-prompt version is ++1.21 pp (p=0.206p=0.206).

Appendix G Hack attempts in LeetCode

Following the grading harness of Wong et al. (2026), we define the attempt rate as the union of the three evaluator categories in which a response defines or modifies run_tests: strict hack, correct with an attempt, and failed attempt. Table 7 reports, over steps 31–40 of each arm, the shares of all responses that are strict hacks, correct, correct with an attempt, correct without one, and attempts. The categories overlap and correctness keeps its usual definition; the attempt label is an observable property of the response, not a measure of intent.

Under the reflected penalty, both low-pass designs remove the attempts along with the strict hacks. Auditing every weak pass with the strong-verdict reward c=bc=b leaves strict hacking at 1.37–21.09% and attempts at 1.80–43.01% across the three seeds (pooled attempt rate 19.96%, exceeding strict hacking by 9.69 pp), whereas auditing every weak pass with 2​b−a2b-a eliminates strict hacking in all three seeds and reduces attempts to at most 0.12%; the difference in late attempts has the same sign in every seed but varies widely across seeds. That correct responses with attempts reinforce the behavior was observed by Wong et al. (2026).

Held-out problems by difficulty.

We sampled 16 responses on each of 353 held-out problems that were never used for RL training, from the starting checkpoint and from the final LB and RB adapters of all three seeds, with the training sampling settings. Problems were split by the dataset’s difficulty label and into thirds of the starting checkpoint’s per-problem correctness (Table 8; bootstrap intervals resample problems conditional on the trained adapters and fixed strata). RB’s strict hacking rises from the easiest to the hardest third by ++29.93 pp [++25.69, ++34.40], while its attempt rate stays between 89.91% and 98.60% in every stratum; strict hacking thus tracks how often an attempt coincides with a failed solution. LB and Full (c=2​b−ac=2b-a) show no resurgence on hard problems. Under Full (c=bc=b), strict hacking is 0.17% on the easiest third with 9.64% attempts, and rises to 4.46% on the hardest third (++4.29 pp [++3.28, ++5.40]).

Appendix H The online rule and a one-step diagnosis at step 120

The online rule estimates, from the audits’ own labels and a smoothed estimate of composition by pass count, how many labels to spend in each group, and may audit only part of a group. It improved JJ over LB in simulation on frozen panels. From the main starting point it fell behind LB early (area under the hacking curve 6.42 pp higher) before both reached near zero. The two arms of a pair did not see identical first-step samples, so the pilot is not a controlled counterfactual for the cause.

At the starting checkpoint of the step-120 pilot, we drew 8 common batches of 16 prompts with 16 responses each from the training distribution, assigned audits to the same responses under LB and under the frozen online rule (penalty −2.5-2.5, p=0.2p=0.2), and computed the exact projections of each response’s score gradient on estimated directions dH=∇P​(H)d_{H}=\nabla P(H) and dC=∇P​(C)d_{C}=\nabla P(C). The directions were estimated by score-function averages with leave-one-out baselines on 864 other prompts with four samples each at temperature 1; their cosine is 0.50. KL, clipping, gradient clipping and weight decay were omitted.

Online minus LB, the hack mass SHS_{H} was −-0.0428 ±\pm 0.0063 (standard error over batches), and the projection of the first-order SGD direction on dHd_{H} was ++0.0003 ±\pm 0.0004. These batches were sampled as in training, with top-pp 0.95, but their scores were evaluated under the full softmax, so the score of a sample does not have mean zero: every response class had a large positive mean projection on dHd_{H} (++27 to ++63). Splits of the difference by response class, or into the change in the std denominator and the direct audit correction, are dominated by this shared component. In these batches the hack responses contributed −-0.0039 ±\pm 0.0009 and the other responses ++0.0042 ±\pm 0.0010, as if the other responses cancelled a stronger correction through the hacks, and the denominator and direct parts were ++0.0006 ±\pm 0.0003 and −-0.0003 ±\pm 0.0003. We repeated the comparison on 8 new batches sampled with top-pp 1, where the class means ranged from −-11 to ++3. The hack mass again differed by −-0.0193 ±\pm 0.0066 and the projection by −-0.0004 ±\pm 0.0006, but the hack responses contributed −-0.0002 ±\pm 0.0003 and the other responses −-0.0002 ±\pm 0.0005, and the denominator and direct parts were −-0.0008 ±\pm 0.0002 and ++0.0004 ±\pm 0.0006. Under both samplers the lower hack mass of the online rule did not produce a detectable difference in the projection, and the attribution to response classes or to the two parts changed with the sampler, so we do not attribute the outcome to any of them. The errors include only the variation over batches, not the error of the estimated directions or of the frozen online state.

Randomly permuting the advantages among the hacks of each group leaves every class coefficient unchanged. Under the online rule the mean change in the dHd_{H} projection was ++0.0002, as it must be by symmetry, but its root mean square over 64 assignments was 0.0024, 2.2 times the mean net projection (−-0.0011); in the batches sampled with top-pp 1 it was 0.0017, 0.85 times the mean net projection (++0.0020). Under LB, which audits whole groups, it was exactly zero. Which hack receives the penalty is therefore a large source of noise in a single update, although its role in the long-run outcome is not identified. We also computed the first step of a fresh Adam state; its projections were too noisy to compare, and since Adam is nonlinear and the omitted terms do not cancel after it, this diagnosis does not identify the optimizer’s contribution.

Appendix I Preregistration and deviations

Each comparison was entered in a dated log, with its arms, primary metric and decision rule, and committed to version control before its runs started. Predictions and their outcomes:

  • •

    The per-item random audit comparison in LeetCode was preregistered without a predicted direction and is reported with two-sided intervals and a seed-level tt-test (Appendix J).

  • •

    The online pilot was preregistered as a test of predictions from frozen-state simulation; the predictions failed.

  • •

    For the Countdown-Code runs of RB and of the group-level advantage correction, we predicted from the sign of the frozen-panel hack mass that RB would not suppress hacking (it did not) and that the group-level correction would (its late hacking of 2.19% fell just short of our 2% threshold; both later seeds suppressed hacking).

  • •

    For seeds 2 and 3 of the LeetCode group-level advantage correction we predicted suppression from the frozen-panel sign; seed 3 suppressed hacking, and seed 2 ended with 3.44% late hacking (partial).

  • •

    LeetCode low budgets: from the sign of the frozen-panel hack mass we predicted that LB would not suppress hacking at 0.1 and would at 0.2 (both held in two seeds), and that LB with corrections scaled by 3.1 and the group-level advantage correction would suppress it at 0.1 (both held). For LB with penalty −11.5-11.5 at 0.1 we predicted no suppression; it suppressed hacking for about 15 steps and then rose again (partial). A continuation from its step 40 rose to 40.5% in steps 31–40, against the prediction of below 10% from the frozen-panel sign at that state.

  • •

    In total, before 16 training runs we predicted from the sign of the frozen-panel hack mass whether hacking would be suppressed (late hacking below 2%) or not (10% or more); 13 predictions held. Besides the runs above, the 16 include seed 1 of the LeetCode group-level advantage correction, the Countdown-Code correction allocated by pass count, and a single-seed LeetCode run of LB with penalty −0.25-0.25 instead of −2.5-2.5; all three were predicted to suppress hacking and did. The three misses (seed 1 of the Countdown-Code group-level correction, seed 2 of the LeetCode one, and LB with penalty −11.5-11.5 at 0.1) all ended between the two thresholds and nearer the predicted one: the first two, predicted to suppress hacking, ended at 2.19% and 3.44%, and the third, predicted not to, ended at 7.9% after suppressing hacking for about 15 steps. The continuation of the last was preregistered with a pair of thresholds outside this count, and its frozen-panel prediction failed (above). Applied to the starting panels of 23 further runs, the same rule matched 20 (Section 5.4).
